sections.headline: Most delivery problems are definition problems.
sections.body: I'm Ankita Pathak. For four and a half years I've worked between stakeholders and delivery teams, defining requirements, prioritising backlogs, and building the reporting that tells everyone where things stand. I trained in business analytics at IIM Indore, then applied it at Codewalla and at WNS (part of Capgemini). Currently a PGCM candidate at Great Lakes Institute of Management, Gurgaon.

sections.title: Agree on it before you build it
sections.body: I start every project by writing down four things: the problem in a sentence, whose problem it is, what is out of scope, and the one number that will tell us it worked. Most of the disagreements that surface in week six come from something nobody wrote down in week one

items.title: Talk to the people doing the workaround
items.note: Ops leads and analysts know where the process leaks. Requirements written from the real routine, not the documented one, survive contact with delivery.

items.title: Put acceptance criteria in the story
items.note: A story that reads clearly can still mean three different things. At WNS, rework fell 20% once each story had to state how it would be checked.

items.title: Settle the definitions before the dashboard
items.note: Agreeing what a KPI counts is worth the argument. Build the chart first and you have only automated the disagreement

sections.title: Open to roles between the business and the build

projects.title: Procurement & Inventory Decision Intelligence Platform
projects.summary: A live decision-support dashboard that turns a Google Sheet into a fully interactive inventory, procurement and supplier intelligence platform — no backend required.
projects.intro: PIDIP consolidates inventory health, procurement recommendations, supplier evaluation, and demand forecasting for a pharmaceutical manufacturer into a single live view. Every number on screen is calculated in the browser from data pulled straight out of a Google Sheet — no server, database, or API keys anywhere in the stack.
projects.objective: Manufacturers often track inventory, consumption, suppliers, and procurement status across disconnected spreadsheets, making it hard to catch a shortage or expiry before it becomes urgent. The goal was to bring all four signals together into one consolidated, always-current decision view — without requiring any backend infrastructure to run it.
did:
Built a client-side decision engine in vanilla JavaScript that reads live data from a 7-tab Google Sheet and computes safety stock status, reorder-point alerts, a weighted multi-criteria supplier score, and a linear-regression demand forecast — entirely in the browser.
Designed a full admin-style Data Console with create/edit/delete access across every table, protected by a session-local editing model: visitor edits are layered on top of live data in the browser's own storage, so the real dataset is never at risk.
Identified and fixed real edge-case bugs during development — including a data-integrity issue where three tables lacked a truly unique row key, a timezone bug in date handling, and a search filter matching against internal IDs — then re-validated the fixes against real data.
projects.resultText: A fully functional, zero-cost platform hosted free on GitHub Pages: six live decision-support views plus a Data Console, all computing in real time from a Google Sheet. Supplier scoring was independently validated by reproducing exact rankings — reliability, lead time, and MOQ — against the full 92-row supplier catalog.
projects.conclusion: PIDIP demonstrates that a genuinely functional, data-driven operations tool doesn't need a traditional backend — a static site, a spreadsheet, and a well-designed client-side engine can deliver real decision support safely and for free.
projects.deckAbout: A quick visual walkthrough of PIDIP's architecture, live decision engine, and the engineering work behind it — including real screenshots and the exact formulas driving each recommendation.

projects.title: Gaming Arena: pricing a venture in three days
projects.summary: Pricing experiments and hourly competitor reads mapped demand instead of guessing at it. Sustained profitability within three days.
projects.intro: A live economics simulation run as a real venture: pricing experiments and hourly competitor reads instead of matching whatever the neighbouring stall charged.
projects.objective: Reach sustained profitability inside a three-day simulation without knowing the demand curve in advance and come out of it able to point at what customers would actually pay, rather than at a hunch that happened to work.
did: Treated day one as measurement rather than trading: deliberate price moves at both ends of the range to find where demand bent.
Tracked competitor pricing hourly and held our position when they undercut, on the read that their volume would not cover the cut.
Reset the price once a day at most, so each move could be attributed to something rather than lost in noise.
projects.resultText: Profitability held for the rest of the simulation, and we finished with a demand curve I could show rather than describe.
projects.conclusion: Spending the first day learning instead of earning felt expensive and was not. The one real failure was record-keeping: the experiments were logged unevenly, so part of what we learned stayed in memory.
projects.deckAbout: Three days of a simulation in a few slides: the pricing experiments on day one, what they revealed about the demand curve, and the decisions that kept profitability holding afterwards.

projects.title: Insurance claim fraud detection
projects.summary: Six models on 20,100 health insurance claims, and the question they all come down to: how many false alarms is one caught fraud worth?
projects.intro: A quarter of these 20,100 health insurance claims are fraudulent, which means a model that flags nothing is already 75% accurate. Six models, one held-out test set, and a threshold table that hands the real decision back to the business.
projects.objective: A quarter of the claims in the dataset are fraudulent, which means a model that flags nothing is already 75% accurate. Accuracy was therefore the wrong thing to optimise. The aim was a ranked review queue an investigator could work through, and a defensible answer to where the threshold should sit.
did:
Explored before modelling. Fraud rate by category showed Specialist Office providers at 50% against roughly 16% elsewhere, Cardiology and Orthopedics at 46%, and elective admissions above emergency ones. Quartiling the numeric fields showed fraud rising with procedure count and provider distance, and flat across patient age. Claim amount peaked in the second quartile rather than the fourth, which is the opposite of where a value-sorted manual queue would look.

Built three features the raw data did not have: days from service to claim, days to policy expiry, and cost per procedure. Dropped the identifiers, since a model can memorise them but they mean nothing for an unseen claim. Oversampled the fraud rows inside the training set only, leaving the test set at its real 25% rate.

Compared six models on one held-out set. Random Forest and XGBoost tied at 0.865 AUC and behaved completely differently: Random Forest is right 89% of the time it flags but misses nearly half the fraud, XGBoost catches more and is wrong more often.
projects.resultText: Cost per procedure, the feature that did not exist in the source data, ranked first in importance, ahead of both fields it was built from. The deliverable was a cut-off table rather than a model: at the default 0.5 threshold the model misses 589 of 1,246 frauds, and dropping to 0.3 catches 994 at the cost of reviewing 1,595 claims instead of 748. Which row is right depends on what an investigation costs against the average payout, so the threshold is the business's decision, not the modeller's.
projects.conclusion:
The model is the easy part. Six of them land between 0.65 and 0.87 AUC in an afternoon, and two tie at the top while behaving nothing alike: one is right nearly every time it speaks and stays quiet through half the fraud, the other catches more and cries wolf more often.

What the work produced is not a prediction but a threshold table. Reviewing 748 claims catches 657 frauds. Reviewing 1,595 catches 994. Choosing between those rows needs two numbers no dataset contains, the cost of an investigation and the size of an average payout, so the last decision belongs to the business and the analysis should stop short of making it.
projects.deckAbout: Read this for the trade-off rather than the score. The threshold table, the feature importances, and the three things the data cannot tell you are all set out in full.

projects.title: Institutional Growth & Market Penetration Strategy
projects.summary: A growth strategy for Skilled Sapiens, repositioning existing Live Projects as credit-mapped institutional internships so the sale moves from discretionary spend to a budgeted regulatory obligation.
projects.intro: A growth strategy for Skilled Sapiens: repackage the existing Live Projects as credit-mapped institutional internships, and sell against a regulatory deadline rather than a voluntary one.
projects.objective:
Skilled Sapiens was selling mentorship to individual students. The sale depended on voluntary decisions, the cycle was long, and institutions treated it as enrichment rather than something they had to buy.
UGC internship guidelines aligned to NEP 2020 changed that. Internships are now compulsory, carrying 60 to 120 hours and 2 to 4 credits, and the obligation is calendared, audited and pre-budgeted. The brief was to work out how Skilled Sapiens could reach institutions. I proposed not building anything new, but repackaging the existing 4 to 12 week mentor-supervised Live Projects against that mandate, and using the free workshops as the way in rather than the product.
did:
Audited the public claims first. The website stated four different mentor counts and three different partner counts across three pages, and the Campus Connect contact button pointed at an unassigned number. Institutional buyers verify before signing an MoU, and contradictory numbers read as inflated. I made reconciling those a prerequisite to any outreach rather than a housekeeping item.

Scored five buyer segments on base size, urgency, ability to pay and how crowded they were. Tier 2 private B-schools in NCR and western UP came out top. Tier 1 institutes scored lowest on willingness to pay but highest on brand value, so I put them in as zero-fee engagements bought with case study rights rather than dropping them.

Mapped the buying centre, because the person who invites you on campus is not the person who signs. Four roles, and the one most often missed is the affiliating university's academic council, which sanctions anything claiming credit. Ignore it and a credit-linked MoU collapses late.

Designed the commercial model around that. Four partnership tiers from free workshop access up to a multi-year alliance, and pricing set at Rs 1,200 to 2,500 per student, deliberately below the fee increment a college can absorb without board approval.
projects.resultText: A three-stage wedge (land with a free workshop, prove with one paid pilot batch, expand to an annual MoU) and a twelve-month roadmap that fixes the product and the website before any outreach begins. Cohort completion rate is the metric I added and would watch hardest: if students do not finish, the compliance value disappears and the account does not renew.
projects.conclusion:
Skilled Sapiens already delivers the thing colleges now have to buy. What changes is who it is sold to and the deadline it is attached to.

Three things carry it. Free workshops buy campus access without needing a budget approval. One paid pilot batch produces the audit trail a TPO can take to the Principal. And cohort completion rate, not enrolment, is what protects the renewal, because a student who does not finish leaves the college out of compliance.
projects.deckAbout: The deck carries the evidence this page summarises: the segment scoring, the website contradictions found in the audit, the four-tier commercial model, and the month-by-month roadmap.
